title: Oxeiptosis in gastrointestinal cancer: molecular mechanisms, therapeutic strategies, and future perspectives.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies represent a major global health burden characterized by high mortality rates, pronounced genomic heterogeneity, and resistance to conventional therapies. While cancer research has historically focused on apoptosis, non-canonical regulated cell death (RCD) pathways have recently emerged as critical regulators of oncogenesis and tumor suppression. Among these pathways, oxeiptosis is a recently identified, non-inflammatory, and caspase-independent cell death mechanism triggered by hyperphysiological levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS). This pathway is mechanistically governed by the mitochondrial Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)/phosphoglycerate mutase family member 5 (PGAM5)/ apoptosis-inducing factor mitochondria-associated 1 (AIFM1) signaling axis. Under conditions of toxic oxidative stress, elevated ROS levels activate Keap1, facilitating the PGAM5-mediated dephosphorylation of AIFM1. This review synthesizes the pathophysiological roles of oxidative stress and the regulatory landscape of oxeiptosis across major GI cancers, including esophageal, gastric, colorectal (CRC), pancreatic, and hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC) 1. Although clinical translation in esophageal and pancreatic cancers is currently constrained by a paucity of direct experimental data, recent multi-omics and bioinformatics analyses have identified oxeiptosis-related gene signatures as robust prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers in gastric cancer and HCC. Furthermore, preclinical evidence demonstrates that small molecules and natural products can successfully exploit the oxeiptotic cascade to bypass established apoptotic resistance. Specifically, the natural compounds sanguinarine and auriculasin trigger potent, PGAM5-dependent oxeiptosis in CRC models, while phenethyl isothiocyanate, dasatinib, and methyl-cantharidimide exhibit strong therapeutic synergy in HCC cell lines. Collectively, targeting oxeiptosis represents a highly promising preclinical strategy to overcome chemoresistance in GI malignancies; however, further in vitro, in vivo, and clinical investigations are essential to validate its therapeutic efficacy and determine whether modulating this pathway translates into improved patient survival and clinical outcomes.

title: Genome-Wide and Multi-Omics Analysis Identified DNA-Interacting Circular RNA circFOXK2 as MLL1 Regulator for Histone H3K4 Methylation in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most devastating malignancies with high lethality despite the current therapeutic interventions. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) play important roles in many biological processes and disease development. However, the underlying mechanism remains largely unexplored. To identify novel druggable targets, we aimed to elucidate the mechanisms contributing to the critical roles of circRNAs in PDAC. We performed a genome-wide and multi-omics investigation on the circFOXK2-DNA interaction in PDAC progression. Single-cell ATAC-sequencing analysis using the publicly available dataset revealed the importance of the circFOXK2-DNA interaction network in intratumoral heterogeneity. Through circRNA-DNA interaction by complementary base pairing, circFOXK2 recognizes targets at different genomic locations: enhancer, promoter, and intragenic region. CircFOXK2 forms a docking pocket by intramolecular base pairing for the N-terminal RNA-recognition motif of PPIE, disrupting the PPIE-MLL1 interaction. This removes the PPIE inhibitory effects on MLL1 for gene-activating H3K4 methylation. Specifically, circFOXK2 promotes TMSB15B and BCAS1 expressions by enhancing H3K4me3 at the promoter. At the gene body, circFOXK2 facilitates transcription elongation of TRIO and LAMA4 by intragenic H3K4me3. At the distal intergenic enhancer, circFOXK2 promotes H3K4me1 of CYP26A1 and TCP11 for gene activation. These results highlight the importance and therapeutic potential of circRNA-DNA interaction in gene regulation.

title: A dual-function XCL1-CD40L mRNA adjuvant potentiates cancer vaccines by coordinating DC recruitment and maturation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the significant promise of mRNA tumor vaccines in treating solid tumors, their clinical response rate is constrained by the low effectiveness of antigen presentation resulting from the immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1) are pivotal in antigen cross-presentation; yet, they frequently exhibit insufficient immune-activating communication within solid malignancies.
METHODS: This investigation comprehensively examined the functional attributes of cDC1 by TCGA cohorts and single-cell transcriptomic data. Guided by these bioinformatic insights, we engineered and synthesized a dual-functional mRNA adjuvant encoding the mXCL1-mCD40L fusion protein. We assessed the biological functions and anti-tumor efficacy of this adjuvant in combination with Glypican-3 (GPC3) and HPV-associated mRNA vaccines via protein expression, structure prediction, in vivo antigen uptake and presentation assays, antigen-presenting cell activation assays, antigen-specific T cell activation tests, and therapeutic studies in tumor-bearing mouse models.
RESULTS: A high cDC1 signature score was associated with improved overall survival across LIHC and SKCM TCGA cohorts. Compared to normal sample, cDC1s in HCC and melanoma retained their antigen-presentation machinery but received reduced activating ligand inputs (XCL1-XCR1 signaling in HCC and CD40-CD40L signaling in melanoma). AlphaFold 3 showed that the mXCL1-mCD40L fusion protein can maintain structural integrity without spatial steric hindrance. The fusion protein was confirmed to be secreted and to retain both XCL1-dependent chemotactic activity and CD40-dependent dendritic-cell activation. mXCL1-mCD40L mRNA-LNP activated macrophages and dendritic cells in vitro, upregulating immune-related gene expression as confirmed by qPCR. In vivo, the dual-functional adjuvant significantly enhanced the anti-tumor effect of the GPC3 vaccine, outperformed co-delivery of separate mXCL1 and mCD40L mRNA-LNP, and induced stronger specific IFN-γ producing T cells. Meanwhile, this adjuvant also boosted the anti-tumor efficacy of HPV-associated mRNA vaccines. Mechanistically, this adjuvant increased tumor-antigen acquisition and cross-presentation by CD103+ DCs and promoted DC maturation in draining lymph nodes, accompanied by an increased proportion of peripheral CD8+ T cells.
CONCLUSION: By enhancing the recruitment and maturation of cDC1s, the dual-function mXCL1-mCD40L mRNA adjuvant boosts the efficacy of GPC3 and HPV-associated mRNA vaccines, supporting its potential as an antigen-flexible adjuvant platform against solid tumors.

title: Disruption of ACTG1 potentiates anti-TIM-3 immunotherapy by reprogramming the immunosuppressive microenvironment via the CSF3/CSF3R axis in pancreatic cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The limited immune infiltration observed in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a major factor contributing to immunotherapy resistance and the consistently poor prognosis. Hence, identifying novel therapeutic targets and developing effective combination strategies to overcome immunotherapy resistance represent urgent and unmet clinical needs.
METHODS: The gene expression datasets and corresponding clinical information were collected from TCGA, GEO and ICGC. The immune cell infiltration (ICI) contents were evaluated by "CIBERSORT". PDAC subtypes based on ICI pattern were obtained from consensus clustering. Their prognostic value was validated by the Kaplan-Meier survival curves. Then, we employed an integrated multi-dataset approach to systematically identify pivotal regulators of PDAC progression. The functional role of ACTG1 was specifically validated through in vivo and in vitro models. The tumor immune microenvironment was characterized by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry (IHC). Potential molecular mechanisms were further investigated using RNA sequencing and tumor cell-macrophage co-culture experiments.
RESULTS: Three distinct immune infiltration subtypes with different prognoses and immunological features were identified in the 608-sample GEO/ICGC training cohort and the 177-sample TCGA-PAAD validation cohort. The ICI pattern with a better prognosis was characterized by high level of plasma cells, activated NK cells, activated DC cells, M1 macrophages and CD8+ T cells, low level of M0 macrophages, M2 macrophages. ACTG1 drives immunosuppression and predicts poor prognosis in PDAC. Mechanistically, ACTG1 promotes tumor cell-derived CSF3 secretion, which upregulates TIM-3 expression on tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) via the CSF3/CSF3R signaling pathway. This cascade reinforces M2-like TAMs polarization and induces CD8+ T cell exhaustion, thereby fostering an immunosuppressive niche. Strikingly, ACTG1 knockdown combined with TIM-3 blockade exerts an enhanced effect in reversing immunosuppression, restoring anti-tumor immunity, and markedly prolonging survival.
CONCLUSIONS: ACTG1 promotes PDAC progression by orchestrating an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment through the CSF3/CSF3R/TIM-3 axis. Thus, combining genetic suppression of ACTG1 with TIM-3 blockade represents a potent therapeutic approach to overcome immune evasion and curb tumor progression.

title: A macrophage-associated immunosuppressive subtype defined by Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium-associated host genes characterizes prognosis and the immune microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium-associated host target genes curated in gutMGene v2.0 may reflect expression programs related to the immune microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but their significance in prognostic stratification and macrophage states remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether operationally defined Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium-associated host genes (LBHGs) can define prognostic subtypes of HCC and reveal the corresponding immunosuppressive macrophage features.
METHODS: LBHGs were operationally defined from Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium-related host target genes in gutMGene v2.0 human records. TCGA-LIHC was used as the discovery cohort for differential expression, univariate Cox, consensus clustering, LASSO-Cox modeling, and survival analysis; GSE76427 was used for expression pattern, subtype projection, and external validation of the risk model; GSE149614 single-cell data were used to calculate the LBHG score, recluster macrophages, and operationally define LBHG-IMac as the subgroup with the highest median LBHG score and significant upregulation of at least 3 prespecified immunosuppressive/pro-tumor markers, representing an LBHG-high immunosuppressive TAM-like macrophage state, and its top-30 marker signature was quantified in TCGA-LIHC and GSE76427 using ssGSEA with within-cohort z-score standardization.
RESULTS: Among 94 cross-cohort detectable LBHGs, 12 core LBHGs were identified. The LBHG subtype constructed based on these genes showed that LBHG-C2 had worse overall survival (OS) (log-rank P = 0.003). The 7-gene risk model effectively distinguished high- and low-risk patients in TCGA-LIHC (log-rank P = 0.001; the 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUCs were 0.744, 0.711, and 0.736, respectively), and risk score was an independent prognostic factor (HR = 1.94, P = 0.005); this model was externally validated in GSE76427 (log-rank P = 0.006; the AUCs were 0.708, 0.691, and 0.721, respectively). Single-cell analysis identified LBHG-IMac as a LBHG-high immunosuppressive TAM-like macrophage state, which was enriched in primary tumors (P < 0.001). LBHG-IMac score was positively correlated with risk score (both P < 0.001), and the high LBHG-IMac group showed worse OS and positive correlations with the expression of immune checkpoint and immunosuppression-related genes.
CONCLUSION: The operationally defined LBHG framework can define an adverse prognostic pattern in HCC and are associated with a LBHG-IMac-enriched immunosuppressive microenvironment.
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

title: Dual targeting of DHODH and SLC29A1 overcomes metabolic resistance and enhances antitumor immune responses in PDAC.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) displays profound metabolic plasticity that sustains rapid proliferation through heightened demands for nucleotide biosynthesis. Here, we characterize HOSU-53 (JBZ-001), a dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) inhibitor demonstrating potent antitumor activity in preclinical PDAC models and define the metabolic determinants of sensitivity and resistance. In HOSU-53-sensitive PDAC cells, DHODH inhibition induces G₂/M cell cycle arrest and triggers apoptotic and ferroptotic cell death. In contrast, resistant cells evade metabolic stress by activating compensatory nucleoside transport and macropinocytosis pathways. Integrated functional and genetic analyses reveal that nucleoside salvage via the equilibrative nucleoside transporter SLC29A1 constitutes a dominant resistance mechanism, enabling uptake of extracellular nucleosides to bypass de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Unbiased metabolomic profiling demonstrates that combined inhibition of DHODH and SLC29A1 precipitates mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, lipid remodeling, and amino acid depletion, culminating in metabolic collapse and energetic failure. Consistent with these findings, dual inhibition markedly suppresses tumor growth and metastatic burden in xenograft and syngeneic orthotopic PDAC models while reprogramming the tumor microenvironment toward a pro inflammatory, immune activated state. Furthermore, co targeting DHODH and SLC29A1 synergizes with anti-PD 1 immune checkpoint blockade, enhancing immunotherapeutic efficacy. Together, these results establish dual targeting of de novo and salvage nucleotide metabolism as a compelling strategy to overcome metabolic resistance, remodel tumor-immune interactions and potentiate therapeutic responses in PDAC.

title: Military Occupation and Incident Cancer in Canadian Armed Forces Personnel and Veterans: A Sex-Stratified Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) includes a large workforce with a diverse spectrum of military occupations and potentially related exposures. The objective was to examine associations between service in distinct military occupations and the subsequent development of cancer.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used CAF administrative data linked to national cancer registry data. Personnel and Veterans with at least 2 years of CAF service between 1990 and 2017 were identified (N = 19,660 females and 129,840 males). Service in common military occupations was categorized using military occupation codes. Associations with incident primary cancer diagnoses (all cancers combined and specific cancer types) between 1990 and 2017 were analyzed using sex-stratified Cox proportional hazards models with age as the timeline for analysis, adjusted for enrollment era.
RESULTS: For most military occupations, no significant associations with all cancers combined or specific cancer types were observed in females or males. Exceptions included occupation as an aviation systems technician, which in females was associated with an increased likelihood of breast cancer, and in males with all cancers combined as well as oral, colorectal, Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and kidney/renal cancers. Positive associations were also observed in females for colorectal cancer in supply technicians, and in males for non-Hodgkin lymphoma in gunners, pancreatic cancer in infanteers, and lung/bronchus cancer in supply technicians.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings can inform health protection measures, benefits and services for military personnel and Veterans. Future research should examine specific factors linked to the increased risks observed.

title: Myeloid Suppressor Cells Drive HCC Invasiveness via the THBS1-SDC4 Pathway.
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) accumulate in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but their activation and tumor-promoting mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated how stromal-myeloid-tumor crosstalk promotes HCC invasiveness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
METHODS: We analyzed single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 36 HCC patients and spatial transcriptomics data from 2 HCC specimens to characterize M-MDSC localization and intercellular signaling. Matrix cancer-associated fibroblast and M-MDSC phenotypes and interactions were assessed using molecular and functional assays. Thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling was investigated in xenografts in immunodeficient mice (n = 8/group) and diethylnitrosamine/carbon tetrachloride-induced HCC in the immunocompetent mice (n = 6/group).
RESULTS: M-MDSCs preferentially localized to EMT-active tumor margins and correlated with EMT activity (Spearman r = 0.30; false discovery rate = 3.3 × 10-4) and shorter overall survival (log-rank P = 0.00124). Matrix cancer-associated fibroblasts promoted M-MDSC activation through collagen-associated CD44 signaling. Activated M-MDSCs induced EMT through thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling, whereas syndecan-4 deficiency suppressed tumor cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and EMT. Thrombospondin-1-deficient M-MDSCs reduced xenograft progression and increased interferon-γ-positive CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytotoxic immune markers in immunocompetent HCC. A thrombospondin communication pathway score was associated with shorter overall survival (log-rank P = 2.28 × 10-5; Cox hazard ratio = 1.23, P = 0.0193).
CONCLUSIONS: Matrix cancer-associated fibroblasts promote monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cell activation, driving epithelial-mesenchymal transition in hepatocellular carcinoma through thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling. Targeting this axis may restrain tumor progression and enhance antitumor immunity.
IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: This study provides mechanistic insight into how M-MDSCs are activated within the HCC tumor microenvironment and subsequently drive tumor cell EMT through THBS1-SDC4 signaling. These findings highlight the importance of tumor-immune-stromal crosstalk in HCC progression and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding the pro-tumor functions of M-MDSCs. The THBS1-SDC4 axis may represent a therapeutically targetable pathway to restrain M-MDSC-mediated tumor aggressiveness and modulate the tumor microenvironment. Further validation in independent clinical cohorts and assessment of therapeutic efficacy are warranted to determine its translational potential.

title: RNA binding motif protein 15 (RBM15) inhibits macrophage phagocytosis via m6A-dependent colony stimulating factor 2 (CSF2)/STAT3 pathway in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a major public health challenge worldwide, marked by difficulties in early diagnosis and a dismal prognosis. The overtly immunosuppressive nature of its tumor microenvironment (TME) renders PDAC largely refractory to existing immunotherapies. Tumor-associated macrophages, the predominant immune infiltrate in the TME, are pivotal in facilitating immune escape. While m6A RNA methylation, the most abundant eukaryotic post-transcriptional modification, is known to contribute to PDAC progression, its specific function in mediating tumor-immune interactions has yet to be fully elucidated. We identify RBM15, a core m6A methyltransferase component, as a key regulator of macrophage phagocytosis in PDAC. RBM15 is notably upregulated in PDAC tissues and is associated with immunosuppressive macrophage infiltration and poor prognosis. Mechanistically, RBM15 binds CSF2 mRNA and enhances its stability in an m6A-dependent manner, thereby increasing CSF2 secretion from pancreatic cancer cells. Tumor-derived CSF2 then activates STAT3 signaling in macrophages, thereby impairing their phagocytic function. In vivo orthotopic models further demonstrate that RBM15 promotes PDAC progression and is accompanied by activation of the CSF2/STAT3 axis and increased immunosuppressive macrophage infiltration. Collectively, our findings reveal a novel non-cell-autonomous mechanism whereby tumor cell m6A modification regulates macrophage function, and provide experimental evidence supporting a potential role of the RBM15/CSF2/STAT3 axis in the immunosuppressive remodeling of the PDAC microenvironment.

title: Correlative insights into luteolin regulating the macrophage-p53-CCNB1/CDK1 axis associated with cell-cycle control in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The polarization of macrophages and the deactivation of oncogenic pathways within the tumor microenvironment are directly linked to the evolution of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a relatively frequent cancer in the world. Though the exact mechanism is yet unknown, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) may alter p53 activity by secreting cytokines. In contrast, the (tumor protein p53, p53) signaling pathway is frequently functionally compromised in HCC as a result of mutation or epigenetic silencing. It is yet unknown if the natural substance luteolin restores p53 function by controlling macrophage polarization, despite its multi-targeted anti-tumor potential.
OBJECTIVE: To clarify the interventional role of luteolin in the evolution of HCC and to uncover the mechanism by which macrophage polarization influences this process via the p53 signaling pathway.
METHODS: The functions of pivotal genes (Cyclin B1,CCNB1), (Cyclin-dependent kinase 1, CDK1), p53 and macrophage polarization-associated factors (Interleukin 6, IL-6), (tumor necrosis factor-α, TNF-α), (Interleukin 10, IL-10), (Transforming growth factor beta 1, TGF-β1) were experimentally verified in conjunction with bioinformatics analysis (screening of luteolin targets for intersection with HCC differential genes and pivotal genes), transcriptome enrichment analysis, immune infiltration assessment, and single-cell sequencing techniques.
RESULTS: 20 hub genes were screened, 5760 HCC differential genes were found, and 104 luteolin action targets were found. According to enrichment analysis, luteolin inhibited HCC via controlling the metabolism of ROS, extracellular matrix catabolism, and cell cycle pathways (p53, cellular senescence). The presence of M2-type TAMs in the tumor core was confirmed by single-cell sequencing, and their secretion of TGF-β and IL-10 led to aberrant activation of CCNB1/CDK1 and cell cycle dysregulation by promoting the ubiquitylation degradation of p53 and inhibiting its nuclear translocation. Luteolin reversed M2-type macrophage polarization, down-regulated IL-10/TGF-β, and was associated with restoration of p53 function via ATM-dependent p53 phosphorylation. This event may induce G2/M-phase arrest and cellular senescence, as well as suppress the activity of the CCNB1/CDK1 complex.
CONCLUSION: Our correlative results suggest that luteolin may reprogram macrophage polarization (inhibiting M2-type and encouraging M1-type), which is associated with relieving IL-10/TGF-β1-mediated suppression of p53 signaling and subsequent inhibition of CCNB1/CDK1-driven cell cycle progression. Nevertheless, the causal direction between macrophage polarization status and p53 function, the primary cellular target of luteolin, protein-level phenotypic validation of macrophage polarization, p53-dependency of CCNB1/CDK1 inhibition, and direct experimental proof for immune escape remain to be fully elucidated. This study highlights the multifaceted impacts of natural medicines in controlling tumor microenvironment and genome stability, and it offers a novel target for combined immune-metabolic therapy of HCC.

title: NicheCorr: Identifying Niche-Specific Differential Gene Co-Expression in Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: Cell-cell communication is central to biological processes such as immune responses and tumor progression, yet the role of spatial proximity between distinct cell types in shaping gene co-expression remains poorly understood. Existing approaches primarily identify differences in average gene expression across tissue regions, often overlooking how local cellular microenvironments reshape gene-gene interactions within cells. To address this gap, we introduce NicheCorr, a statistical procedure that identifies cell type-specific niche-associated gene co-expression changes within distinct spatial niches. In simulations, NicheCorr attained the highest power for detecting niche-dependent co-expression. It was also the only method evaluated that maintained Type I error control when mean expression varied nonlinearly with the niche, a setting in which CS-CORE, scHOT without mean adjustment, and the Pearson test all exhibited inflated false positive rates. Furthermore, NicheCorr integrates ligand-receptor (LR) inference, enabling a comprehensive view of spatially structured signaling interactions. We applied the framework to the CosMx SMI Human Liver FFPE Dataset and the Xenium Human Pancreatic Cancer Dataset, identifying 52 gene pairs in liver tumor cells whose co-expression changes with T-cell niche composition and 48 gene pairs in pancreatic cancer whose fibroblast niche-dependent co-expression differs between tumor and CFTR- tumor cells, and uncovering potential LR interactions that may underlie these differential co-expression patterns.

title: Keratin 17 Defines an Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition-Associated Migratory Cell State in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by early invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance that contribute substantially to its poor clinical outcome. Keratin 17 (K17) is a recognized marker of the aggressive basal-like subtype of PDAC and an independent predictor of adverse prognosis; however, the biological basis for this association remains incompletely understood. To define K17-associated cellular programs, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 42 patients, Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) proteomic data from 140 tumors, MACSima multiplex spatial imaging of 63 patients, dual-plex immunohistochemistry of 60 cases, and three-dimensional spheroid migration assays. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-associated gene programs among K17-positive malignant epithelial cells. Consistent with this finding, K17-positive tumors in the CPTAC cohort exhibited enrichment of the Hallmark EMT pathway at the protein level. Among six candidate markers identified through transcriptomic analyses, laminin subunit gamma-2 (LAMC2) was the only candidate associated with K17 at every validation step. Tumors positive for both K17 and LAMC2 had significantly worse overall survival than double-negative tumors (adjusted hazard ratio = 2.53). Multiplex spatial imaging localized K17-positive cells predominantly to poorly differentiated tumor regions and demonstrated frequent single-cell co-expression with LAMC2. Whole-slide dual-plex immunohistochemistry further confirmed the association between K17 and LAMC2 and showed progressive enrichment of K17/LAMC2-positive tumor cells with increasing intratumoral histologic grade. Functionally, gain- and loss-of-function studies in three-dimensional PDAC spheroids demonstrated that K17 promotes migratory outgrowth, and differences in proliferation did not account for this effect. Collectively, these findings identify K17 as a marker of a poorly differentiated, EMT-associated migratory cell state in PDAC and provide functional evidence that K17 contributes to tumor-cell migration.

title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
abstract: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested, because doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies. Given a source manuscript and a target scRNA-seq dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, and reports which findings transfer and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.
